new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngwi is a two-tone (H/L) language; the only prominence claim in the primary literature is that the stem-initial (root-initial C1V1) syllable is the prosodically prominent position (consonant contrasts are fullest there; C2 and noun-class prefixes are treated as prosodically weaker), in line with stem-initial prominence elsewhere in West-Coastal/NW Bantu. No source states an explicit word-stress rule or describes stress acoustically.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The companion paper (Pacchiarotti & Bostoen 2021, Language in Africa 2(3): 53-54) adds only that C2 'can therefore be considered as a prosodically less prominent position than C1 in a C1V1C2V2 template' and that 'the word-initial prefix position is also prosodically less prominent than the stem-initial C1 position' (both inferred from diachronic consonant loss). PiHPh pp.134-135 speak of historical CVCV words having become 'a monosyllabic CVː stressed word'.
new_statements.domain_note: Prominence is located relative to the (noun/verb) stem, not the word: prefixes are outside the prominent position. Most synchronic stems are monosyllabic C(G)VC after final-vowel loss, so stem-initial = only stem syllable in the majority of words. Statement is hedged ('might be directly related to the fact that...') and framed comparatively; it is not an instrumental or explicit synchronic stress description. Variety: Eastern Ngwi of Mangai.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern sources (Pacchiarotti, Maselli & Bostoen 2021; Pacchiarotti & Bostoen 2021, 2024, 2025) describe Eastern Ngwi as spoken in Mangai (approx. -4.02, 19.53, left bank of the Kasai), from two consultants recorded in Idiofa in 2019 (BantuFirst project). The authors note that Western Ngwi (Kamtsha-Loange; Bwantsa Kafungu 1979, Kumpel Wossey 1980/2001 'ngwi engye/ɛngyɛ') shows 'remarkable differences... certainly with respect to phonology'. Glottolog ngul1247 'Ngwii' [nlo] covers both; Glottolog's own lgcode annotations call the described variety 'Eastern Ngwi'.

sources.locator: Section 2 '(Supra)segmental and phonotactic features of Ngwi', p.110 (supporting: pp.134-135; and Pacchiarotti & Bostoen 2021, Language in Africa 2(3), pp.53-54)
sources.note: Sec. 2 (p.110): consonant distribution asymmetry attributed to stem-initial position being 'a position of phonetic and phonological prominence' (as in other WCB / NW Bantu); two tonemes H and L (+R, F contours), heavy functional load, no phonemic vowel length. pp.134-135: historical CVCV > 'a monosyllabic CVː stressed word'. No explicit rule for where word stress falls.

sources.citation: Pacchiarotti, Sara & Koen Bostoen. 2021. The evolution of the noun class system of Ngwi (West-Coastal Bantu, B861, DRC). Language in Africa 2(3): 11-67.
sources.note: pp.53-54: C2 in a C1V1C2V2 stem 'can therefore be considered as a prosodically less prominent position than C1' (citing Hyman 1998, 2008), and prefix loss is regular 'if we posit that the word-initial prefix position is also prosodically less prominent than the stem-initial C1 position' -- diachronic inference of stem-initial prominence, not a stress rule.

sources.note: Tone only: two-way underlying H/L contrast, lexically and grammatically contrastive; contour tones on heavy CVC syllables with phonetic lengthening; vowel length 'primarily a function of the number of tones on a vowel' (p.161). No mention of stress/accent/prominence anywhere (grep: stress, accent, prominen = 0 hits).
